client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I try to sit down and focus on work, these memories of her just come flooding in and I can't concentrate on anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because nothing is really going to change the fact that she's gone.
therapist:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief this fresh and this present makes complete sense, and those memories flooding in are a sign of how deeply you loved her. You're right that nothing will change the fact that she's gone, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to fix that or take the pain away. What I *can* offer is a space where you don't have to carry this alone, even just for a little while.

Can you tell me a little about what those moments feel like when the memories come — is it more sadness, longing, something else entirely?

client: It's mostly longing, I think — like there's this hollow feeling in my chest when I remember her voice or the way she used to hum while she cooked. But then the guilt creeps in right after, because I keep thinking about the last few months when I was so busy with work that I didn't visit as much as I should have. It's hard to just sit with the sadness when the guilt keeps pulling me back to all the things I didn't do.
therapist: That hollow feeling you're describing is such a tender, human way to grieve someone you loved, and it makes so much sense that her voice and those small moments are what you miss most. The guilt is worth gently exploring together, though — when you say you didn't visit "as much as you should have," I'm curious where that "should" is coming from, because our minds can be very harsh judges during grief, often holding us to a standard we'd never apply to someone else we cared about. If a close friend told you they'd been overwhelmed with work while their grandmother was ill, what would you say to them?

client: I know what I'd say to a friend — I'd tell them they were doing their best, that life gets complicated, that their grandmother knew they loved her. But it feels completely different when it's me, like that logic just doesn't apply the same way. I can't shake the feeling that I had chances I let slip by, and no amount of reframing that seems to make the guilt actually go away.
therapist: What you're noticing is actually really important — you can *see* the compassionate logic clearly, but it doesn't yet *feel* true for yourself, and that gap between knowing and feeling is one of the most painful places to be. The guilt may not disappear through reframing alone, and that's okay; sometimes it also needs to be honored as part of love, a sign of how much she mattered to you rather than proof that you failed her. I don't want to rush past that feeling, but I am curious — when you imagine your grandmother herself looking back at those last months, what do you think *she* would have said about the kind of grandchild you were to her?

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I know what she would have said — she always told me I was her favorite, that I made her laugh, that she loved when I visited. But it's hard to let that in, because it feels like I'm just... letting myself off the hook too easily, like I'm using her kindness to avoid facing what I actually did or didn't do. She was generous like that, my grandmother, and part of me worries I'm just hiding behind her generosity now.
therapist: The fact that you're so resistant to "letting yourself off the hook" actually tells me a lot about your integrity — someone who truly didn't care wouldn't be sitting with this much pain. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: accepting her love and her perspective isn't hiding behind her generosity, it's actually honoring her by trusting that she knew you and meant what she said. What would it mean for *you* — not for her memory, not as an excuse — but for you personally, if you allowed even a small part of her view of you to be true?

client: I sat with that for a second and... it actually kind of got to me, which I wasn't expecting. If even a small part of what she saw in me were true, I think it would mean I'm not as fundamentally broken as I feel like I am most days. But then this voice immediately comes in and says "you're just looking for permission to stop feeling bad," and I don't know how to tell the difference between genuine healing and just... letting myself off too easy.
therapist: That moment of something getting through — that's not nothing, and I want you to stay with it for just a second, because it sounds like a quiet but important truth trying to reach you. The voice that calls it "looking for permission" is worth examining too, because there's a difference between *avoiding* grief and *not punishing yourself indefinitely* — genuine healing doesn't mean the loss stops mattering, it means you can carry it without it destroying you. I'm wondering, when you imagine what "letting yourself off too easy" would actually look like in practice, what are you afraid might happen if you stopped holding yourself so tightly to account?

client: I think what scares me is that if I stop holding myself accountable, I'll just... forget her. Like the guilt is the only thing keeping the connection alive, and without it I'll drift away from who she was and what she meant to me. It sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it genuinely feels like letting go of the pain means letting go of her.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like grief trying to protect love, and that's a very human thing to do. But I want to offer a gentle observation: the memories you described earlier — her humming, her voice, the way she called you her favorite — those aren't made of guilt, they're made of warmth and connection, and they were there before the guilt arrived. What if the things that truly keep her alive in you aren't the painful feelings, but exactly those tender details you carry so naturally?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it almost feels too easy, like if I let go of the guilt, I'm somehow admitting I didn't care enough when she was actually here. The warm memories feel good for a second, but then the guilt rushes back in like it's correcting me, reminding me of all the times I didn't call, didn't visit. I guess I'm just not sure I trust that the love can survive without the pain holding it in place.
therapist: The image of guilt "correcting" you is so telling — it's as though some part of you has appointed it as a guardian of your love for her, making sure you never forget the weight of what she meant to you. But I want to sit with something you said: you've described her voice, her humming, her laughter, the way she made you feel like her favorite — none of that needed guilt to bring it forward, it came from somewhere much deeper and more lasting. What if the love was never in danger of disappearing, and the guilt has just convinced you that it's the one keeping the lights on?

client: That's... a really strange way to think about it, and honestly it kind of stops me in my tracks. Because part of me wants to say yes, you're right, the memories came on their own — but then there's this other part that immediately panics and thinks, what if I let the guilt go and I actually do start to forget her? I know that probably sounds irrational, but it feels like a real risk, like loosening a grip on something I can't afford to drop.
therapist: That panic makes complete sense, and I don't want you to rush past it or dismiss it as irrational — it's telling you something important about how much she matters to you. But I'd gently invite you to notice that you've now spontaneously described her humming, her cooking, her laughter, her exact words to you, the feeling of being her favorite — all of that arrived without guilt summoning it, just from us talking about her with care. What if the real question isn't whether you can afford to loosen the grip, but whether you might actually be able to hold her *more fully* once the guilt isn't crowding her out?

client: That actually... stopped me for a second, because I hadn't noticed I was doing that — just talking about her like she was right here. But I think part of me is scared that if I stop feeling guilty, it means I've accepted that she's gone, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that to be true. The guilt almost feels like it's keeping her alive somehow, like letting it go would be the final goodbye.
therapist: What you just named is so profound and so tender — the guilt hasn't just been about accountability, it's been a way of holding on, of refusing to close a door that part of you isn't ready to close yet. And I want you to know that's not weakness or irrationality, that's love doing the only thing it knows how to do when it's faced with an unbearable loss. But I'm curious — when you were just talking about her naturally, describing her so vividly, did that feel like saying goodbye, or did it feel like she was somehow still with you?

client: Honestly... it felt like she was still with me, at least for a moment. Like I could almost hear her laughing at something I said, the way she always did when I got too serious about things. But then I caught myself and the guilt came rushing back, like I wasn't allowed to have that feeling without it costing me something.
therapist: That moment — her laughing at you for getting too serious — that's her, fully alive in you, and no amount of guilt created that; it came from decades of love that isn't going anywhere. I want to gently name what I think is happening: the guilt rushing back in like a toll booth, insisting that joy has to cost you something, may actually be getting in the way of the very connection you're so afraid to lose. What do you think she would have made of the idea that you're only allowed to feel close to her if you're suffering?
